For each integer \(n\ge2\), let \(\mathcal K_n\) consist of all sets \(K=\overline\Omega\subset\mathbb C^n\), where \(\Omega\) is a nonempty bounded connected open set with \(C^\infty\) boundary.

Use the following orientation convention for pseudoconvexity. Near each \(q\in\partial K\), take a smooth real defining function \(\rho\) with \(K\cap U=\{\rho\le0\}\) and \(d\rho\ne0\) on \(\partial K\cap U\). The boundary \(\partial K\) is pseudoconvex if, at every such \(q\),
\[
\sum_{j,k=1}^{n}\rho_{z_j\bar z_k}(q)v_j\overline{v_k}\ge0
\qquad\text{whenever}\qquad
\sum_{j=1}^{n}\rho_{z_j}(q)v_j=0.
\]

An open set \(Y\subset\mathbb C^n\) is called Oka if, for every integer \(m\ge1\), every nonempty compact convex set \(Q\subset\mathbb C^m\), every holomorphic map \(f:V\to Y\) on an open neighbourhood \(V\) of \(Q\), and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there is a holomorphic map \(F:\mathbb C^m\to Y\) satisfying
\[
\sup_{x\in Q}\|F(x)-f(x)\|<\varepsilon,
\]
where the norm is Euclidean.

Define the two sets of dimensions
\[
\begin{aligned}
S&=\bigl\{n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}:\ \text{for every }K\in\mathcal K_n,\quad
\partial K\text{ pseudoconvex}\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathbb C^n\setminus K\text{ Oka}\bigr\},\\
N&=\bigl\{n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}:\ \text{for every }K\in\mathcal K_n,\quad
\mathbb C^n\setminus K\text{ Oka}\ \Longrightarrow\ \partial K\text{ pseudoconvex}\bigr\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Determine exactly the ordered pair \((S,N)\).

One necessary implication can be proved directly:
\[
\boxed{2\in N.}

Here is its proof, including the computational verification I performed.

### 1. A consequence of the stated Oka property

Every continuous plurisubharmonic function on an Oka open set \(Y\) that is bounded above is constant on each connected component.

Indeed, let \(B\Subset Y\) be a Euclidean ball. Apply the approximation property to the inclusion of \(\overline B\) into \(Y\), obtaining entire maps
\[
F_\nu:\mathbb C^n\longrightarrow Y,\qquad F_\nu\longrightarrow\operatorname{id}
\quad\text{uniformly on }\overline B.
\]
If \(u\) is continuous, plurisubharmonic, and bounded above on \(Y\), then \(u\circ F_\nu\) is a bounded-above plurisubharmonic function on \(\mathbb C^n\). Restriction to complex lines and the subharmonic Liouville theorem show that it is constant. Passing to the limit gives \(u(x)=u(y)\) for \(x,y\in B\). Thus \(u\) is locally constant.

### 2. A strictly pseudoconvex boundary point gives an obstruction

Suppose an open set \(Y\) has a smooth strictly pseudoconvex boundary point \(q\), with local defining function \(r\) oriented so that \(Y=\{r<0\}\).

Replacing \(r\) by \(r+Ar^2\), for sufficiently large \(A>0\), makes its full complex Hessian positive definite at \(q\), without changing the local domain. Taylor expansion then provides a holomorphic quadratic polynomial \(h\), with \(h(q)=0\), and constants \(c,\delta>0\), such that
\[
\operatorname{Re}h(z)\le -c\|z-q\|^2
\qquad
(z\in\overline Y,\ \|z-q\|<\delta).
\]
Choose \(0<\eta<c\delta^2/4\). The function
\[
u(z)=
\begin{cases}
\max\{\operatorname{Re}h(z),-\eta\},&z\in Y\cap B(q,\delta),\\
-\eta,&z\in Y\setminus B(q,\delta)
\end{cases}
\]
is well-defined, continuous, plurisubharmonic, and bounded. The displayed estimate makes it identically \(-\eta\) in an annular neighbourhood of the gluing sphere. It approaches \(0\) near \(q\), so it is nonconstant on the adjacent component of \(Y\).

Consequently, \(Y\) cannot be Oka.

### 3. Application in complex dimension two

Let \(K\in\mathcal K_2\), and suppose its boundary is not pseudoconvex. At some boundary point its Levi form is negative on a nonzero complex tangent vector. The complex tangent space is one-dimensional, so the Levi form of the exterior defining function \(-\rho\) is positive definite there.

Thus \(\mathbb C^2\setminus K\) has a strictly pseudoconvex boundary point and, by the preceding argument, is not Oka. Taking the contrapositive proves \(2\in N\).

assert s.simplify(
